messages.subject: Confusion regarding multisession models and single session models
messages.subject_clean: Confusion regarding multisession models and single session models
messages.body_plain:
Hi!
I am estimating the densities of tigers and leopards in Central India using MLSECR. I have used both single session and multiple session SECR models to estimate the densities. The estimates are coming different in the two cases (although the confidence intervals are overlapping). I am little confused about this. Can you please tell me why this might be the case?

Additionally the models which are being selected in single session and multiple session are different. In case of tigers, the best model for the all sessions using single session models were (D~1,g0~h2,sigma~1). For tigers, the best model in multiple session SECR was (D~session,g0~h2+session,sigma~h2+session). In case of leopards, the best models were (D~1,g0~h2,s~1) and (D~1,g0~1,s~h2) in session 1 and both sessions 2 & 3 respectively. When multiple session models were run for the same dataset, the best model as per AIC value as (D~session,g0~h2+session,sigma~h2+session). I am a little confused about the reason behind this.

I have also used sex of the identified individuals as a covariate  for hybrid mixture models: secr.fit(TCH, mask=pmask,binomN =1,model = list(D~1,g0~1,sigma~1), hcov='sex', verify=F). Can this individual covariate used to estimate sex-specific density?

Thanks in advance,
Anindita

messages.subject: Re: Confusion regarding multisession models and single session models
messages.subject_clean: Confusion regarding multisession models and single session models
messages.body_plain:
Hi Anindita
You should expect different models (single session vs multi-session) to give different estimates, but the difference will be large only if the data are sparse (or session differences large and unmodelled).
I can't see quite what your issue is with model selection (your second paragraph).
The hybrid mixture models estimate a parameter 'pmix' that is the sex ratio - not quite sex-specific density, but perhaps OK?
Murray

messages.subject: interpretation of pmix parameter in modelling sex-specific parameters with hcov
messages.subject_clean: interpretation of pmix parameter in modelling sex-specific parameters with hcov
messages.body_plain:
Hi all!
We're analysing camera trapping data to estimate density and related parameters of a snow leopard population. Since we could assign sex to 18 out of 23 detected individuals, we modelled sex-specific encounter prob and sigmas by using hcov=Sex (2 levels with missing values NAs).

Brief summary of data for clarity:

Occasions 106, Detections 177, Animals 23, Detectors 61
Number of movements per animal:
 0  1  2  3  4  5  6  7  8 11 15 18
 3  1  1  5  4  2  2  1  1  1  1  1
Individual covariate Sex: f 7, m 11, NAs 5
Number of sex-specific detections (+ 18 unknown): f 47, m 112

We're having troubles regarding the interpretation of the pmix parameter and sex-specific encounter probability estimates. Specifically, since we have more males and more male-detections, we expected higher encounter prob for males..(which I got when modelling the encounter prob only). But in our final best model, where both g0 and sigma are sex-specific, g0 seems higher for females:

                         beta              SE.beta               lcl         ucl
D                -10.21789767 0.63540416 -11.46326694 -8.97252839
D.Sl               1.18378967 0.27875357   0.63744271  1.73013663 ## continuous cov
g0               -3.39325184 0.20906714  -3.80301590 -2.98348777
g0.h2m       -0.56682429 0.24983264  -1.05648726 -0.07716132  ## lower for males?
g0.D              0.21023990 0.08716978   0.03939028  0.38108952 ## continuous cov
sigma          7.59393697 0.09053109   7.41649929  7.77137465
sigma.h2m   0.76062321 0.10963194   0.54574855  0.97549787  # higher for males, ok
pmix.h2m    0.05518827 0.44281840  -0.81271985  0.92309639

Is it possible? Any suggestion?
Additionally, I’m not sure how to interpret the pmix parameter estimate: pmix.h2m<-plogis(coef(bestmod)[8,1]) # 0.51
Is it the probability of an individual in the pop being male?

Thank you so much,
Valentina

messages.body_plain:
OK - if not due to sparse data there must be something odd (and probably wrong) about your implementation. The need for multisession models is usually obvious from the structure of the data (e.g. separate blocks of sampling in time or space), although sometimes 'sessions' can be used for subgroups within one population (e.g. sexes). We just don't know enough about what you are doing. Feel free to try again with more detail and a specific question.
Murray

messages.subject: Re: interpretation of pmix parameter in modelling sex-specific parameters with hcov
messages.subject_clean: interpretation of pmix parameter in modelling sex-specific parameters with hcov
messages.body_plain:
Hello Valentina
Thanks for your clear data summary. I take it you are using a current version of 'secr'? Yes, your fitted model seems to have lower g0 for males, but they also have larger sigma, which makes sense I think if you read Efford and Mowat 2014 <https://www.otago.ac.nz/density/pdfs/Efford%20and%20Mowat%202014%20Ecology.pdf>. The class-specific estimates of g0, sigma and pmix are given on the natural ('real') scale by predict (bestmod, all.levels = TRUE). This should give the same result you got manually from plogis(coef(bestmod)[8,1]) (= invlogit(coef(bestmod)[8,1])).And yes that is the probability of being male.
Murray

messages.body_plain:
I guess the 'all.levels' option sets up far too many combinations with your continuous covariates. You might need to manually set the levels for which you want predictions - using the newdata argument of predict(). As a general aside: the model matrices in 'secr' work better with covariates that have just a few levels (faster, less memory required).
Murray

messages.subject: Number of Occasions only reported as 1 for a 45 night survey?
messages.subject_clean: Number of Occasions only reported as 1 for a 45 night survey?
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am busy running a density estimate analysis for spotted hyaena from a 45 night camera trap study with 30 sites. On some days the sites were inactive and I have incorporated this into the 2013trapfile.txt as usage.

Using the below script and the attached two txt files I run the secr.fit function.

CaptHist <- read.capthist("2013RHScaptfile.txt", "2013trapfile.txt", detector="proximity", fmt="trapID", skip = 1)
CaptHist
summary(CaptHist)

fit <- secr.fit (CaptHist, buffer = 8000, trace = FALSE)
fit

My concern is two fold.

1) I receive the warning:
> fit <- secr.fit (CaptHist, buffer = 8000, trace = FALSE)
Warning message:
In bias.D(buffer, temptrps, detectfn = output$detectfn, detectpar = dpar,  :
  bias.D() does not allow for variable effort (detector usage)

Do you know why this might be the case? Do I need to worry about it and how can I address this?

2) When I look at the summary of the fitted model I see the following...
Detector type      count
Detector number    30
Average spacing    3020.741 m
x-range            379440.9 411743.9 m
y-range            6867394 6893572 m

 Usage range by occasion
     1
min 41
max 45

N animals       :  79
N detections    :  159
N occasions     :  1
Count model     :  Binomial, size from usage
Mask area       :  117969 ha

I do not understand why my N Occasions is 1? Surely it should be 45 and will this effect the analysis?

Any advice would be greatly appreciated!

Best,
PJ

messages.subject_clean: Interpretation of goodness of fit test
messages.body_plain:
Hello secr users,

I would like to check overdispersion of my dataset vs my top-ranked model. I have looked up several times the secr manual and the different threads of this group related to the topic, but I am still unsure about it, so I am turning to you for guidance.

>From what I understood, I would need to run a goodness of fit test on my top-ranked model using secr.test and the statfn function given in the example, i.e:
bothfn <- function(object)
                { CH <- object$capthist
                f1 <- sum(apply(abs(CH) > 0, 1, sum) == 1) / nrow(CH)
                devdf <- deviance(object) / df.residual(object) c(f1 = f1, devdf = devdf)
                }
test <- secr.test (secrdemo.0, nsim = 19, statfn = bothfn, fit = TRUE) test plot(test, main = '')
With secrdemo.0, I get the following results:
                    P
f1            0.65
devdf      0.60

Which means that the rank of the observed value in the vector combining the observed value and simulated values is 12. This is where I get stuck. How do you link these probabilities to goodness of fit and overdispersion? The greater P(devdf ), the better the fit?

Apologies if my question seems obvious.

Best wishes

Marie

messages.subject: Re: Number of Occasions only reported as 1 for a 45 night survey?
messages.subject_clean: Number of Occasions only reported as 1 for a 45 night survey?
messages.body_plain:
1. secr.fit() by default runs the function bias.D() as an approximate post-hoc check for truncation bias (buffer too narrow). The check is described briefly at ?bias.D. You can suppress the check with biasLimit = NA. bias.D() does not take 'usage' into account, hence the warning, but this is usually a trivial issue.
2. In recent versions of 'secr' the default for many models is to collapse multi-occasion data to a single occasion (see e.g. secr-version4.pdf <https://www.otago.ac.nz/density/pdfs/secr-version4.pdf>). This can be much faster. I regret the confusion it has caused, but the deed is done. Suppress using  details = list(fastproximity = FALSE).
Murray

messages.subject: Re: Interpretation of goodness of fit test
messages.subject_clean: Interpretation of goodness of fit test
messages.body_plain:
I think you can interpret P as the probability of observing a value that large under the null hypothesis that the data were generated under the fitted model. So small P (<0.05?) implies significant lack of fit. There is no canned measure of overdispersion. Goodness-of-fit and overdispersion have yet to be fully investigated for SECR models: I'm not claiming expertise here, just providing a tool.
Murray

messages.subject: Bug in make.capthist for multi detectors
messages.subject_clean: Bug in make.capthist for multi detectors
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

Just wanted to query whether this is a possible bug in secr 4.3.3 or I am misunderstanding something.

I found some unusual behaviour when using make.capthist with multi detectors. It reported a warning that it was "dropping repeat detections within occasions at exclusive detectors (traps)" when I was sure I had removed all such repeat detections.

Find attached a script that reproduces the problem for a minimal example and proposes where I think the problem is in make.capthist.

Best,

Richard

messages.subject: Re: Bug in make.capthist for multi detectors
messages.subject_clean: Bug in make.capthist for multi detectors
messages.body_plain:
Hi Richard
It's a bug, of course. Thanks for your detailed report. I have fixed it in the pre-release version available here secr_4.3.4.zip <https://www.otago.ac.nz/density/zip/secr_4.3.4.zip> (Windows binary) or here secr_4.3.4.tar.gz <https://www.otago.ac.nz/density/zip/secr_4.3.4.tar.gz> (source).
As a workaround, you can also read data as if from a "proximity" detector and then convert to "multi":
traps<- make.grid(detector = "proximity")
chp <- make.capthist(captures, traps)
chm <- reduce(chp, outputdetector = "multi", dropunused = FALSE)
The result is not identical but the differences are subtle and I think ignorable.
Murray
